What should tourists not do in Egypt?

Tourists should avoid photographing military or security sites, bringing drones without permission, disrespecting religious places, climbing restricted monuments, touching ancient carvings, drinking alcohol publicly, or making offensive comments about local customs, religion, or politics.
Do tourists need to dress modestly in Egypt?

Yes, modest clothing is recommended in cities, local neighborhoods, mosques, and religious sites. Beachwear is fine at resorts and pools, but shoulders and knees should usually be covered when visiting traditional or sacred places.
Can tourists take photos in Egypt?

Yes, photography is allowed in many tourist areas, but restrictions apply at some museums, tombs, military sites, and government buildings. Always check signs, follow staff instructions, and ask permission before photographing local people.
Is bargaining allowed in Egypt?

Bargaining is normal in traditional markets and souvenir bazaars, but not in supermarkets, restaurants, pharmacies, or shopping malls. Keep the conversation polite, and if you agree on a price, it is respectful to complete the purchase.
Can tourists drink alcohol in Egypt?

Yes, alcohol is available in many hotels, licensed restaurants, resorts, and Nile cruises. However, public drinking and drunken behavior are not appropriate and can be considered disrespectful, especially outside tourist areas.

Most rules are based on respect and common sense. Follow local customs, dress appropriately, obey photography restrictions, respect historical sites, and listen to guides or officials. Most tourists who do this travel comfortably without problems.

What Are the Rules for Tourists in Egypt?

Visiting Egypt isn't about following a long list of strict rules.

It's more about understanding the country's culture and showing a little respect for local traditions.

Millions of visitors travel to Egypt every year without any problems because the expectations are actually quite straightforward. Dress appropriately when needed, respect historical sites, ask before photographing people, and use common sense in public places.

Most travelers quickly discover that Egyptians are welcoming, friendly, and happy to help visitors who show genuine respect for their culture.

The biggest mistakes usually happen because people simply don't know what is considered normal.

Something that feels perfectly acceptable at home may attract unwanted attention in another country. Learning a few basic customs before you arrive can make your trip smoother, more enjoyable, and far more comfortable.

In this guide, we'll explain the most important rules and cultural expectations every tourist should know before visiting Egypt.

Respect Local Culture

Egypt is a modern country with world-famous tourist destinations, but it is also a society where traditions remain important.

In hotels, beach resorts, and tourist areas, you'll generally notice a relaxed atmosphere. Outside those places, especially in residential neighborhoods or religious areas, local customs become more visible.

The easiest approach is simple.

Observe how local people dress and behave, then follow the same level of respect.

You don't need to change your personality.

Just remember that you're a guest in another culture.

Dress Modestly in Certain Places

One of the questions travelers ask most often is whether there is a dress code.

The answer depends on where you are.

Location Recommended Clothing
Beach resorts Normal beachwear
Hotel pools Swimwear
City sightseeing Comfortable, modest clothing
Mosques Shoulders and knees covered
Local neighborhoods Respectful casual clothing

Women do not normally need to cover their hair unless entering a mosque where head coverings may be required.

Men should also avoid entering religious sites wearing sleeveless tops or very short shorts.

Dressing respectfully isn't about strict rules.

It's about showing courtesy toward local customs.

Photography Has Some Important Limits

Egypt offers incredible photography opportunities, but there are a few rules worth knowing.

Personal photography with phones and standard cameras is generally allowed at tourist attractions and public places. Professional filming equipment or large commercial setups may require permits.

More importantly, avoid photographing:

  • Military buildings
  • Police facilities
  • Government installations
  • Security checkpoints
  • Certain infrastructure

It's also polite to ask permission before photographing local people, and extra care should be taken around children.

Leave Your Drone at Home

This is one rule that surprises many visitors.

Egypt has very strict regulations regarding drones.

Tourists should not bring recreational drones into the country because they may be confiscated, and unauthorized possession can lead to legal consequences.

If aerial photography is part of your travel plans, it is far better to enjoy professional photos or licensed aerial footage than risk bringing your own drone.

Respect Ancient Monuments

The pyramids and temples have survived for thousands of years because they are carefully protected.

Visitors should never climb monuments unless clearly permitted, touch ancient carvings unnecessarily, or remove stones or artifacts from archaeological sites.

Even small actions that seem harmless can contribute to long-term damage.

Take photographs.

Admire the history.

Leave everything exactly where you found it.

Public Behavior Matters

Egypt is generally more conservative than many Western countries.

That doesn't mean tourists are expected to follow complicated rules, but modest public behavior is appreciated.

Very public displays of affection are uncommon outside tourist resorts, loud arguments attract attention, and respectful conduct is always the safest approach.

A smile, patience, and politeness go a long way.

Be Respectful During Ramadan

If your visit falls during Ramadan, daily life may feel slightly different.

Many local people fast from sunrise until sunset, so restaurants, cafés, and business hours can change.

Tourists are still welcome to eat and drink, especially inside hotels and tourist restaurants, but avoiding food or drinks directly in front of people who are fasting is considered thoughtful.

Once the sun sets, cities often become lively again as families gather for evening meals.

For many visitors, Ramadan becomes one of the most memorable cultural experiences of the trip.

Bargaining Is Part of the Experience

In traditional markets such as Khan el-Khalili, bargaining is perfectly normal.

It isn't considered rude.

Instead, it's often viewed as part of the shopping experience.

The key is to negotiate politely and keep the conversation friendly.

If the price doesn't work for you, simply thank the seller and continue walking.

There's rarely any need for confrontation.

Many travelers actually find bargaining becomes one of the more enjoyable parts of visiting local markets.

Stay With Licensed Tour Providers

Whether you're booking a Nile cruise, a desert excursion, or airport transfers, choosing licensed companies makes the experience much smoother.

Reliable operators usually provide better vehicles, experienced guides, clearer schedules, and proper local support.

For travelers who want everything organized from arrival to departure, Egypt guided tour packages can remove much of the uncertainty while allowing you to focus on enjoying the journey rather than arranging logistics.

Understand Tipping Etiquette

Tipping is part of daily travel in Egypt, especially in tourism.

You may hear the word baksheesh, which refers to a small tip or gratuity. Hotel porters, drivers, guides, restaurant staff, restroom attendants, and cruise staff often receive tips for helpful service.

The easiest way to handle this is to keep small Egyptian pound notes with you.

You do not need to tip everyone excessively, but small gestures are appreciated when someone provides service. Having smaller notes also avoids the awkward situation of wanting to tip but only carrying large bills.

Be Careful With Public Conversations

Egypt is generally welcoming to tourists, but visitors should still be thoughtful about sensitive topics.

Avoid public political discussions, criticism of religion, or disrespectful comments about local customs. What may feel like casual conversation at home can be misunderstood in another cultural setting.

This does not mean you need to be nervous.

Just keep public conversations respectful and avoid topics that may create tension.

Travel is much easier when curiosity is paired with sensitivity.

Alcohol Rules for Tourists

Alcohol is available in many hotels, resorts, licensed restaurants, and Nile cruise ships.

However, public drinking is not part of everyday local culture and should be avoided. Being visibly drunk in public can create problems and is considered disrespectful.

If you drink alcohol, do so in appropriate venues and remain discreet.

In Red Sea resorts, the atmosphere is usually more relaxed, while Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan feel more conservative in public areas.

Rules Around Mosques and Religious Sites

Mosques are beautiful places to visit, but they require respectful behavior.

Before entering, you may need to remove your shoes. Women may be asked to cover their hair, and both men and women should cover shoulders and knees.

Inside religious sites, speak quietly, avoid interrupting worshippers, and follow any instructions given by staff.

Even if you are visiting as a tourist rather than for religious reasons, the space remains sacred for local people.

Respectful behavior is always noticed.

Money and Shopping Etiquette

In Egypt, some prices are fixed and others are negotiable.

Supermarkets, pharmacies, hotel shops, restaurants, and shopping malls generally use fixed prices. Traditional bazaars and souvenir shops often allow bargaining.

Place Bargaining?
Supermarkets No
Pharmacies No
Restaurants No
Shopping malls No
Local markets Yes
Souvenir bazaars Usually yes

The golden rule is simple: bargain where it is expected, not everywhere.

If you agree on a price, it is polite to complete the purchase.

Safety Rules Tourists Should Follow

Most visits to Egypt are smooth, especially on organized routes covering Cairo, Luxor, Aswan, and the Red Sea. Still, the usual travel precautions matter.

Keep your passport secure.

Use licensed transport.

Avoid carrying large amounts of cash.

Stay aware in crowded markets.

Follow advice from your guide, hotel, or local representative.

Common Mistakes Tourists Make in Egypt

Most mistakes are small and easy to avoid.

Some visitors dress too casually in religious or local areas. Others photograph people without asking, bring drones without understanding the rules, or underestimate how strong the sun can be during sightseeing days.

Another common mistake is treating archaeological sites like outdoor theme parks.

These places are part of world heritage. Walking carefully, respecting barriers, and following site rules helps protect them for future visitors.

A respectful traveler almost always has a better experience.

How to Behave at Historical Sites

Historical sites in Egypt can feel open and spacious, but they are carefully protected.

Do not climb restricted monuments.

Do not touch painted walls or carvings.

Do not remove stones, sand, or fragments.

Do not cross barriers for photos.

Even if no one immediately stops you, these actions can damage fragile heritage.

The best photographs are the ones taken without harming the place you came to admire.

Tourist Rules Are Mostly Common Sense

The rules for tourists in Egypt are not difficult.

Dress respectfully when needed, ask before photographing people, follow security instructions, respect religious spaces, avoid sensitive public discussions, and protect archaeological sites.

That is most of it.

Egypt does not ask visitors to be perfect.

It simply asks them to be aware.

When you travel with respect, local interactions usually become warmer and more enjoyable.

Travel Through Egypt With Confidence and Respect

A successful Egypt trip is not only about seeing the pyramids, temples, and Nile. It is also about understanding how to move through the country respectfully and comfortably. Small details—what to wear, where to take photos, when to tip, and how to behave at sacred or historic places—can make the journey feel much smoother.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should tourists not do in Egypt?

Tourists should avoid photographing military or security sites, bringing drones without permission, disrespecting religious places, climbing restricted monuments, touching ancient carvings, drinking alcohol publicly, or making offensive comments about local customs, religion, or politics.

Do tourists need to dress modestly in Egypt?

Yes, modest clothing is recommended in cities, local neighborhoods, mosques, and religious sites. Beachwear is fine at resorts and pools, but shoulders and knees should usually be covered when visiting traditional or sacred places.

Can tourists take photos in Egypt?

Yes, photography is allowed in many tourist areas, but restrictions apply at some museums, tombs, military sites, and government buildings. Always check signs, follow staff instructions, and ask permission before photographing local people.

Is bargaining allowed in Egypt?

Bargaining is normal in traditional markets and souvenir bazaars, but not in supermarkets, restaurants, pharmacies, or shopping malls. Keep the conversation polite, and if you agree on a price, it is respectful to complete the purchase.

Can tourists drink alcohol in Egypt?

Yes, alcohol is available in many hotels, licensed restaurants, resorts, and Nile cruises. However, public drinking and drunken behavior are not appropriate and can be considered disrespectful, especially outside tourist areas.

Are tourist rules strict in Egypt?

Most rules are based on respect and common sense. Follow local customs, dress appropriately, obey photography restrictions, respect historical sites, and listen to guides or officials. Most tourists who do this travel comfortably without problems.
